title: Kalshi: Two Edges, One Research Machine
subtitle: Liquidity incentives, the discretionary research desk, and what the evidence says to build next
description: A review of the Kalshi bot's two newest research tracks: the liquidity-incentive market-making thesis and the discretionary market research desk. The episode separates what has actually been built and measured from what remains hypothetical, then lays out the next evidence-gathering steps before either approach should scale.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: This is Build OS Radio. Today we are opening up the Kalshi bot, but not to talk about one trade. The interesting story is that the project has started splitting into two very different ways of looking for edge. One is the liquidity incentive strategy: get paid, in theory, for supplying useful resting liquidity. The other is the discretionary market research desk: research a small number of markets deeply, make at most a few tiny decisions, and build a record of whether the research actually beats the price.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: And those two approaches are almost opposites. The incentive strategy tries to care less about predicting the final event and more about market microstructure. The desk does the reverse. It says forget automating every market. Find the handful where outside information, settlement mechanics, or a stale price might give us a better estimate than the crowd.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Which is a meaningful change from the original idea of a bot that just keeps discovering strategies and trading them.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Right. The repo is becoming more like a research laboratory with multiple economic hypotheses. The code is still important, but the real product is increasingly the evidence system around the code: pre-registered gates, raw market data, reward accounting, a trade ledger, postmortems, and explicit reasons not to scale.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Start with the liquidity incentive strategy. What is the thesis in plain English?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Kalshi can run liquidity incentive programs that reward participants for posting qualifying orders. So instead of saying, I know whether this contract resolves yes or no, the thesis says: maybe we can earn enough incentive credit by maintaining useful quotes that the reward offsets fills, fees, adverse selection, and the capital tied up in the position.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: So it is closer to running a tiny market-making business than betting on the outcome.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Exactly, but the phrase tiny market-making business hides the hard part. A displayed reward pool is not the same thing as our reward. We need to know how the scoring works, how much competing depth is ahead of us, whether one side or both sides actually fill, how long we are left with one-sided exposure, and whether the reward survives the losses caused by being the person other traders choose to hit.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: And that is why Phase Zero became so elaborate.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Yes. The repo built a read-only shadow instrument that discovers active incentive programs, watches the live order book and trade tape, simulates several quote policies across multiple capital tiers, and evaluates fills under optimistic, conservative, and queue-aware models. It records marks after a fill, paired and single-leg economics, program terms, settlement, and collector health. The key design decision is that the promotion criteria read the conservative model. The optimistic model is there to show the ceiling, not to give permission.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: The early result was not flattering.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: No. The estimated reward number could look very good while the actual mechanics underneath it looked bad. Early shadow reads had essentially no conservative two-sided pairs completing. Even when optimistic pairs appeared, the two legs could be separated by something like seventeen minutes. That is not a neat market-making round trip. That is a long interval where you are exposed on one side and available to be adversely selected.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Which creates an important distinction: a model can calculate a large incentive reward while the trading process that is supposed to earn it does not yet exist in the data.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: That distinction has probably been one of the best lessons from this workstream. Estimated reward is not realized reward. A both-filled event is not the same thing as two independent fills twenty minutes apart. And a positive headline produced by an unvalidated share model is not evidence of profitability.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Then the build shifted. Instead of only simulating, we added a tiny live capability.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: A one-sided smoke test, with deliberately narrow limits. One resting maker bid, one contract, a low price cap, a small total committed budget, and hold to settlement. The point was not to prove the full two-sided thesis. It was to prove that the real order path, queue behavior, fills, and incentive eligibility could be observed with actual money without turning the experiment into a meaningful bankroll risk.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: That sounds almost too small to learn anything economically.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: It is too small to establish profitability, and the repo says so. But it is large enough to validate plumbing and to answer a more basic question: can a very small book actually earn any measurable incentive credit? If the answer is no, scaling a beautiful reward formula is pointless.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Which led to the reward ledger.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Yes. The repo discovered a frustrating measurement problem: the API exposes program terms, but not a clean field saying, here is the exact liquidity reward your account earned in this interval. So the project added an append-only balance ledger and calculates a residual. Balance change is reconciled against settlements, sell proceeds, buy cost, and fees. Anything unexplained becomes a candidate incentive residual, not automatically a reward.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Candidate is doing a lot of work there.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: It has to. A deposit could look like a giant positive reward. A missing fee could create a negative drift. A partial portfolio read could create nonsense. So the ledger tags suspicious windows rather than converting every unexplained cent into victory. That is the right philosophy because the signal we are hunting may literally be pennies.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: The other important discovery was that not all incentive markets look remotely alike.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: That may be the biggest strategic shift. Competing depth at the best bid varied by orders of magnitude. Some programs had only a handful of contracts competing at the touch while others had thousands. Whatever the exact reward-share function is, a thinner queue is directionally more attractive than a massive queue if all else is equal.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: And the original live universe was not choosing based on that.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Correct. The live runner was effectively prioritizing programs by when they ended, not by whether the reward looked economically winnable. That means the experiment could be perfectly implemented and still test the wrong markets. The repo has now separated those questions: first prove the reward accounting, then test thin-book programs where a one-contract participant has a plausible chance of getting a non-trivial share.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: We also got a newer signal from the fill data. The conservative both-fill rate moved from roughly half a percent to around one-point-eight percent, and the markets pinned from the live book filled both sides much more often than the rest of the shadow population.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Yes, but the repo handled that carefully. The pinned sample was basically two markets from one event, so it would be wrong to generalize that into a universal rule like short-dated markets fill better. More importantly, even after removing the pinned markets, the non-pinned fill rate also increased. That second movement is still unexplained. So the result is useful as a clue, not as permission to rewrite the thesis after the fact.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: And the headline economics were still not a clean green light.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: No. One recent conservative read still had the five-hundred-dollar tier materially negative on the main policy, even though some policy cells looked positive. The correct interpretation is that the instrument is finally generating better evidence, not that the strategy has been proven.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Now switch to the market research desk. This came from a different idea entirely: instead of asking the bot to trade constantly, ask the system to behave like a full-time researcher and only surface a few decisions.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: The desk is almost an anti-bot. Three researched picks per day is the ceiling, not the target. The position is tiny. The operator places it manually. Every pick is written into a ledger before the action. Every loss gets a postmortem. And an edge class can be closed after enough observations if it does not beat its break-even requirement.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Why keep the human in the loop if the research itself can be automated?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Because the bottleneck is currently epistemic, not mechanical. We do not need millisecond execution. We need to know whether the research process can identify mispriced contracts at all. Manual placement removes a huge amount of execution complexity while we learn. If the desk eventually shows repeatable edge, automation becomes a separate engineering decision rather than an assumption baked into the experiment.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: What did we actually build for it?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: A board-reading script that scans open markets and surfaces things like spread, volume, time to close, and fees. A ticker deep-dive mode that can inspect rules, order book, and recent trades. A bounded source-fetch tool that can read approved public settlement or reference sources. A ledger and postmortem record. And now the desk is a formal session role in the repo, with a playbook and handoff so a future research session can resume the process instead of reinventing it.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: There were some mundane bugs early on too.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: And those are worth mentioning because they demonstrate why the desk needed tools instead of pure web browsing. The first board scan read old field names and thought current markets had zero volume. Then a one-hundred-cent ask exposed a formatting assumption in the fee helper. The order book endpoint used a fixed-point key the reader was not accepting. Those were not economic failures, but any one of them could have contaminated a decision if the output had been trusted blindly.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Then the research pipeline started looking at things like fuel prices, mortgage rates, central-bank data, and OpenRouter usage markets.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Right. The desk is deliberately source-specific. The question is not, what do I feel about this market? It is, what exact data resolves this contract, what public source approximates or predicts that data, what is the current market price, and what assumptions bridge the source to settlement? The recent work even added a no-pick result after the tools were functioning. That is important. A research desk that must trade will manufacture confidence.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: So compare the two theses. What is the incentive strategy betting on, intellectually?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: It is betting that there is an economic transfer available for performing a service: supplying qualifying liquidity. The uncertainty is mostly about scoring, competition, fills, adverse selection, and whether a tiny participant can capture enough of the pool.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: And the desk?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: It is betting that careful information work can occasionally produce a better probability estimate than the market. Its uncertainty is about calibration, source quality, settlement interpretation, selection bias, and whether a few apparent wins are skill or noise.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Which means the two systems fail differently.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Exactly. The incentive strategy can fail even if our event forecasts are perfect, because it may simply be impossible for our size to win meaningful reward without taking bad fills. The desk can fail even with flawless execution because our research may not be better than the price. That difference is useful. These are genuinely different edge classes, not two versions of the same strategy.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: So what are the recommended next steps for the incentive workstream?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: First, finish the measurement loop before scaling. Let the reward ledger accumulate through completed programs and reconcile any residual cents against known cash movements. We need at least one clean case where a program ends and the accounting says, with reasonable confidence, this is the reward we earned.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Second?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Make market selection part of the experiment explicitly. The thin-book discovery is too important to leave as an accidental observation. Pre-register a ranking that includes competition depth, program terms, distance from the scoring reference, time remaining, and expected capital at risk. Then compare it against the old soonest-ending universe without retroactively moving the gate.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: And the both-fill problem?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Keep measuring it, but stop assuming two-sided completion is necessarily the only viable form. The one-sided smoke test exists because the data has repeatedly shown that one side is easier to fill than a safe pair. If incentive credit can be earned one side at a time with bounded downside, that may become a different strategy with its own thesis. Do not rescue the original two-sided thesis by quietly redefining it.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: There is also that unexplained rise in the non-pinned fill rate.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: That deserves its own investigation. Was the market population changing? Was there a time-of-day effect? Did program age change? Did the collector behavior alter eligibility or observation windows? Until that is decomposed, the new fill rate should be treated as a measurement to explain, not a parameter to optimize around.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: What about the desk?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: The desk needs volume of evidence, not volume of trades. Keep the three-per-day ceiling, but allow zero. Every pick should carry a pre-trade probability, market price, edge class, source list, and the exact settlement interpretation. After settlement, score the probability, not just win or loss. A seventy-percent call that loses is not automatically bad research, and a fifty-one-percent call that wins is not automatically good research.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: So build calibration, not a victory counter.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Yes. And aggregate at the edge-class level. Fuel data, macro releases, usage metrics, weather, or whatever categories emerge should earn the right to continue based on repeated evidence. Thirty independent observations is still not a magical threshold, but it is much more informative than three memorable wins. If an edge class is below break-even after its pre-registered sample, close it or redesign it rather than explaining it away.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Would you automate placement next?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Not yet. I would automate research reproducibility first. Make every desk recommendation re-runnable from a saved source snapshot and rule set. Then automate market discovery, candidate scoring, and the research brief. Manual execution is cheap friction right now. The bigger risk is that a future session cannot reproduce why a recommendation existed.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: There is one broader move that seems to connect everything. The Kalshi repo is slowly becoming a portfolio of experiments rather than a single bot.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: I think that is the right mental model. You have prediction strategies, execution research, liquidity incentives, and a discretionary desk. They should share accounting and evidence standards, but they should not share excuses. Each thesis needs its own mechanism, failure mode, and promotion gate.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: Which suggests the next dashboard should maybe not ask, how much did the bot make?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: It should ask, what did we learn per dollar of risk and per week of experiment time? A strategy that loses five dollars but conclusively kills a bad thesis can be more valuable than one that makes three dollars through noise. Especially at this stage, the scarce resource is not capital. It is clean information.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: So if you had to describe where the project stands today in one sentence?

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: The Kalshi bot is no longer searching for one clever strategy. It is building a disciplined process for discovering which kinds of edge are real, which are illusions, and how cheaply we can tell the difference.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: And for the next iteration, the target is not bigger bets. It is better evidence: verified incentive credits, better market selection, more independent fill observations, reproducible desk research, and enough settled picks to judge calibration.

dialogue.speaker: guest
dialogue.text: Exactly. If either strategy is real, the evidence should become harder to explain away as the sample grows. If that does not happen, the system should be designed to tell us early.

dialogue.speaker: host
dialogue.text: That is Build OS Radio. Two edge hypotheses, one research machine, and a much more interesting Kalshi project than a bot that simply trades more often.
